title: L: Python cell options and svg
text:
NoteAbout this page



This page tests the panzoom extension with the Jupyter engine: the same cell options as the R pages, on matplotlib figures. knitr and Jupyter hand figures to Quarto differently (knitr writes the image markdown itself; Jupyter cells come back as notebook outputs), so the filter has to find the figures and their cell options either way. The document has no lightbox: key, and only marked cells should open the viewer.
Rendering it needs Python with matplotlib and ipykernel: see tests/README.md.
Jupyter leaves the panzoom and lightbox options out of the code shown on the page (knitr shows them); the Code button at the top shows the full source.
Headings carry what the browser test checks, as on the other pages: expect-open, expect-hint, expect-max-zoom, expect-fit and expect-format (svg: the viewer got a vector image).
The cases below share this setup and helper:
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def walk(ax, n=200, title=None):
    ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=n)))
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
```

title: L: Python cell options and svg

```{python}
#| fig-cap: A sine wave.

x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
plt.plot(x, np.sin(x))
plt.show()
```

title: L: Python cell options and svg
text:
6. Wide collage (8 × 0.8 in)
A strip, so it opens at screen height. Jupyter figures are shown at their size in inches × 96 px (Quarto writes it on the image), not shrunk to the column as knitr’s are: a 25 × 2 in collage would be 2,400 px wide on the page, cut off at the column’s edge. This one fits.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: An 8 × 0.8 inch collage of 8 panels.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 8, figsize=(8, 0.8), layout="constrained")
for ax in axes:
    walk(ax)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=4)
plt.show()
```




An 8 × 0.8 inch collage of 8 panels.

section: 11. panzoom and lightbox options on one cell
text:
11. panzoom and lightbox options on one cell
Both options: panzoom wins, and the lightbox: options are dropped. (With Jupyter, Quarto’s lightbox ignores #| lightbox: with options under it anyway, unlike with knitr; lightbox: true works, as in case 9.)

```{python}
#| fig-cap: 'Both options: panzoom.'

plt.plot(x, np.sin(6 * x))
plt.show()
```




Both options: panzoom.

title: L: Python cell options and svg
text:
12. matplotlib as svg
The same figure path as case 1, written as svg instead of png: Jupyter saves the figure file itself, unlike knitr (svg from R is on E: image formats). The viewer redraws svg at each zoom, so it stays sharp. Jupyter ignores a cell’s fig-format, so the cell switches matplotlib’s output to svg itself, and back to png after.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: A damped wave, as svg.

%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["svg"]
plt.plot(x, np.exp(-x / 4) * np.sin(3 * x))
plt.show()
%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["png"]
```




A damped wave, as svg.

title: J: Python lightbox reference
text:
NoteAbout this page



This page is the reference for page K: Python (Jupyter) cells rendered with Quarto’s built-in lightbox only, lightbox: true, and no panzoom filter. It shows what Quarto does with each case; K renders the same cases with panzoom: true as well. The knitr equivalents are pages A and C.
Keep the cases in step with the other page of the pair. Each heading’s expect-open says what should open. Jupyter leaves the panzoom and lightbox options out of the code shown on the page; the Code button at the top shows the full source.
The cases below share this setup:
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
```

text:
4. Nested lightbox: options
A cell’s own lightbox: options ask for Quarto’s lightbox, so panzoom leaves the cell to it, as with knitr (page C, cases 6 and 7). With Jupyter, Quarto’s lightbox ignores the options themselves: the group and description don’t reach it.

```{python}

plt.show()
plt.plot(x, np.cos(3 * x))
plt.show()
```


text:

Without the panzoom filter (K) the option means nothing, and the document’s lightbox: true takes the plot.

```{python}
plt.show()
```

title: H: wide and tall figures
text:
2. Wide collage with fit: contain
The override for case 1: the whole collage, as a strip.

```{r}

#|   fit: contain
#| fig-width: 25

```




The collage, forced to open whole.

title: H: wide and tall figures
text:
3. Moderately wide figure (16 × 4 in)
Wide, but readable whole: the size rule leaves it alone.

```{r}

#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "A 4:1 figure."

```

title: H: wide and tall figures
text:
4. Tall strip (4 × 15 in)

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 15
#| fig-cap: "A tall strip of 8 panels."

set.seed(2)
par(mfrow = c(8, 1), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:8) plot(cumsum(rnorm(100)), type = "l", main = paste("Row", i), xlab = "", ylab = "")
```




A tall strip of 8 panels.

title: H: wide and tall figures
text:
5. Large poster (24 × 18 in)
Opens whole; zoomed in, it extends past the screen both ways, and Shift+scroll moves sideways.

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 24
#| fig-height: 18
#| fig-cap: "A 24 × 18 inch poster of 48 panels."

set.seed(3)
par(mfrow = c(6, 8), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:48) plot(cumsum(rnorm(100)), type = "l", main = paste("Panel", i), xlab = "", ylab = "")
```




A 24 × 18 inch poster of 48 panels.

text:

A portrait photo.

title: H: wide and tall figures
section: 8. fit: height on an ordinary plot
text:
8. fit: height on an ordinary plot
On a screen wider than the plot (1.4:1), filling the height is already the whole plot, so this opens like fit: contain and can’t zoom out. Case 10 shows fit: height on a figure where it differs.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: height

wave(k = 3)
```

title: H: wide and tall figures
section: 9. fit: width on an ordinary plot
text:
9. fit: width on an ordinary plot
Filling the width makes the plot taller than the screen: it opens closer than the whole plot, and zooms out to it.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: width

wave(k = 4)
```

title: H: wide and tall figures
section: 10. fit: height on a wide figure (12 × 4.5 in)
text:
10. fit: height on a wide figure (12 × 4.5 in)
Not a strip (shown whole it is over a quarter of the screen tall), so fit: auto would open it whole. fit: height opens it filling the screen height (but not past its real size), from where it was clicked, and zooms out to the whole figure.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: height
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

collage(n = 6)
```

title: H: wide and tall figures
section: 11. Case 10 with a long caption and description
text:
11. Case 10 with a long caption and description
The caption and description sit below the image; fit: height fills the height left above them, so it opens smaller than case 10. The caption scrolls past a quarter of the screen, the description past a fifth, so the image keeps at least about half.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: height
#|   description: "A long description, to take room below the image. Each panel is a random walk of 200 steps, drawn with base R's `plot()` in a one-row layout (`par(mfrow = c(1, 6))`), coloured along the `hcl.colors()` palette. The figure is 12 by 4.5 inches, which knitr writes at 192 dpi (2304 by 864 px). With `fit: height` the viewer opens it as tall as the space above this text allows, and no taller than its real size. Drag or use the arrow keys to move along the figure, scroll or press - to zoom out to the whole of it, and 0 to come back to this opening view."
#| fig-cap: "Six random walks side by side, opened with `fit: height` under a long description."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

collage(n = 6)
```




Six random walks side by side, opened with fit: height under a long description.





A long description, to take room below the image. Each panel is a random walk of 200 steps, drawn with base R’s plot() in a one-row layout (par(mfrow = c(1, 6))), coloured along the hcl.colors() palette. The figure is 12 by 4.5 inches, which knitr writes at 192 dpi (2304 by 864 px). With fit: height the viewer opens it as tall as the space above this text allows, and no taller than its real size. Drag or use the arrow keys to move along the figure, scroll or press - to zoom out to the whole of it, and 0 to come back to this opening view.

title: F: options
text:
NoteAbout this page



This page tests panzoom’s options one at a time: opting out with .nopanzoom and #| panzoom: false, and the per-cell hint and max-zoom options. The page itself sets loop: true, so the gallery in case 6 wraps around. There is no lightbox, so an image panzoom leaves alone opens nothing. The caption and description options are on G: captions and descriptions, fit on H: wide and tall figures.
Each case says what to expect in its heading’s attributes (expect-open, expect-hint, expect-max-zoom), or on a single image, and the browser test checks them.
The cases below draw with this helper:
```{r}
wave <- function(k = 1) {
  x <- seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 400)
  plot(x, sin(k * x), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = hcl.colors(4)[k],
       main = paste("Wave", k), xlab = "x", ylab = "sin(kx)")
}
```

title: F: options
text:

text:
6. Gallery with loop: true
Three plots in one gallery. With the page’s loop: true, ← on the first goes to the last, and “previous” is never disabled.

```{r}
#|   group: waves
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "Wave one."
#|   - "Wave two."
#|   - "Wave three."

wave(k = 2)
wave(k = 3)
```

title: D: panzoom filter, no document lightbox key (selective mode)
text:
NoteAbout this page



This page tests the panzoom extension. The panzoom filter is on, and the images marked with .panzoom or #| classes: panzoom should open the pan/zoom viewer. The document has no lightbox: key, so Quarto’s lightbox only applies where a case asks for it (the #| lightbox: cell options in cases 6 and 7). Case 6’s first chunk has both on purpose: panzoom should win, and its #| lightbox: options are dropped, so it doesn’t join GLightbox’s gallery. Case 9’s link should still work (images inside links are left alone).
Compare each case with the same numbered case in a-lightbox, which renders the same cases with Quarto’s lightbox alone.

title: panzoom
text: This is a Quarto extension that opens figures in a full-screen viewer, built on Panzoom: scroll to zoom toward the cursor, drag to pan, double-click or 0 to reset, Esc to close. It attempts to match, and extend, the feature set of Quarto’s built-in lightbox. Source and documentation: https://github.com/sekoclancy/panzoom.

title: panzoom
text:
Chunk output
Mark a code cell with #| panzoom: true. Click the figure to open it, scroll to zoom toward the cursor, drag to pan, double-click to reset, Esc to close.

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4

image(volcano, col = hcl.colors(100, "Viridis"), asp = 1 / 3)
```

title: panzoom
text:
Cross-referenced figure
Labeled figures work too (Figure 1). Options under #| panzoom: override the document’s settings for one cell: this figure zooms to 10 instead of the page’s 6, and hides the hint.

```{r}
#| label: fig-volcano
#| fig-cap: "Maunga Whau volcano."
#| panzoom:
#|   max-zoom: 10
#|   hint: false

filled.contour(volcano, color.palette = terrain.colors)
```







Figure 1: Maunga Whau volcano.

text:
Markdown image

![A markdown image with the `.panzoom` class.](images/volcano.png){.panzoom}



A markdown image with the .panzoom class.

title: panzoom
text:
Captions and galleries
The viewer shows the figure’s caption. Plots with the same group form a gallery: use the previous and next buttons, ←/→ or a swipe to step through them. Subfigures of one figure are a gallery automatically.
```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   group: volcano-views
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "Volcano heights as an image."
#|   - "The same data as a perspective plot."
#| layout-ncol: 2

image(volcano, col = hcl.colors(100, "Viridis"))
persp(volcano, theta = 135, phi = 30, col = "green3", shade = 0.5, border = NA)
```






Volcano heights as an image.







The same data as a perspective plot.





```{r}
#| label: fig-volcano-sub
#| fig-cap: "Two views of Maunga Whau, as subfigures."
#| fig-subcap: ["Contours", "Filled contours"]
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| panzoom: true

contour(volcano)
image(volcano)
```











(a) Contours











(b) Filled contours







Figure 2: Two views of Maunga Whau, as subfigures.

title: panzoom
text:
Wide figure
A figure many times wider than tall would be too thin to read if it opened whole, so it opens at screen height, at the spot you clicked: click one of the panels below and the viewer opens on it. Drag or use ←/→ to move along it; zooming out shows the whole figure.

```{r}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-width: 25
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-cap: "Twelve random walks, side by side."

set.seed(1)
par(mfrow = c(1, 12), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:12) plot(cumsum(rnorm(200)), type = "l", main = paste("Panel", i))
```




Twelve random walks, side by side.

title: panzoom
text:
Math in captions and descriptions
Captions and descriptions keep their math, typeset as on the page, along with citations, cross-references and links.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "The standard normal density, $\\varphi(x)$."
#| panzoom:
#|   description: "$\\varphi(x) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} e^{-x^2/2}$. The shaded area is $P(|X| < 1) \\approx 0.683$."

x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400)
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "x", ylab = "density")
inner <- abs(x) < 1
polygon(c(-1, x[inner], 1), c(0, dnorm(x[inner]), 0), col = "grey85", border = NA)
lines(x, dnorm(x), lwd = 2)
```




The standard normal density, \(\varphi(x)\).





\(\varphi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2}\). The shaded area is \(P(|X| < 1) \approx 0.683\).

title: panzoom
text:
Untouched figure
Without the option, Quarto’s own lightbox still handles the figure.

```{r}

```

title: panzoom
panzoom
text:
Test pages

R
The same 12 lightbox situations (galleries, subfigures, captions with math, images in links, margin images, …) rendered four ways:

A: R lightbox reference: Quarto’s built-in lightbox alone.
B: marked images + lightbox: the usual setup, lightbox: true with some images marked for panzoom.
C: panzoom match: auto: panzoom picks the images itself.
D: explicit marking: images marked with .panzoom or #| classes: panzoom.

And pages of their own:

E: image formats: webp, svg and pdf output.
F: options: opting out, and the hint, max-zoom and loop options.
G: captions and descriptions: citations and cross-references, and the caption and description options.
H: wide and tall figures: 25 × 2 inch collages, tall strips and other shapes, and the fit option.
I: wide figures in galleries and layouts: the same collages and strips in galleries and layouts.



Python

J: Python lightbox reference: Quarto’s lightbox alone on Python cells.
K: Python, panzoom: true with the lightbox: the same cells, with panzoom taking the images the lightbox would.
L: Python cell options and svg: the R pages’ cell options on matplotlib figures, and svg output.

title: E: image formats
text:
NoteAbout this page



This page tests the panzoom extension with the knitr graphics devices used in practice: webp, svg and pdf output, for a wide collage and a standard plot. Every figure is marked with #| panzoom: true and should open the pan/zoom viewer, except where a case says otherwise. Figure shapes and how they open are on H: wide and tall figures.
Headings carry what the browser test checks: expect-fit (the opening view: contain, height or width), shift-scroll (which way Shift+scroll moves the image: x, y or none) and expect-scale="1" (opens at real size, not enlarged).
webp comes from ragg’s agg_webp device: knitr has no built-in webp device, and agg_webp needs units = "in" because knitr passes sizes in inches.
The cases below draw with this helper (ragg writes the webp files):
```{r}
library(ragg)

# A collage: `n` panels side by side, like a wide patchwork figure.
collage <- function(n = 12) {
  set.seed(1)
  par(mfrow = c(1, n), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(cumsum(rnorm(200)), type = "l", main = paste("Panel", i),
         xlab = "", ylab = "", col = hcl.colors(n)[i], lwd = 2)
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "A 25 × 2 inch collage of 12 panels (webp)."
```

6. png + cairo_pdf (dev: [png, cairo_pdf])
Like case 5, with the cairo PDF device, which embeds fonts and handles Unicode (µ, Greek letters) and transparency better than pdf. The page shows the png either way. With a PDF device alone, there is no image to open: Quarto embeds the PDF in a small box with the browser’s PDF viewer, which panzoom leaves alone.

title: G: captions and descriptions
text:
NoteAbout this page



This page tests citations and cross-references in the viewer. A caption is copied from the page, so whatever Quarto renders there comes through. A description is rendered with the page too, in a hidden block the viewer copies, so its citations resolve, its cross-references get numbers, and a work cited only in a description is still listed under References. Quarto’s own lightbox shows a citation in a caption as raw [@key] (quarto-cli#10709).
Cases 1–5 have the expect-references attribute: the viewer must show at least one citation or cross-reference, none unresolved, and each must link to something on this page. Cases 6 and 7 test the per-cell caption and description options (expect-caption).
The cases below draw with this helper:
```{r}
wave <- function(k = 1) {
  x <- seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 400)
  plot(x, sin(k * x), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = hcl.colors(4)[k],
       main = paste("Wave", k), xlab = "x", ylab = "sin(kx)")
}
```

section: 6. Collages of different lengths in a gallery
text:
6. Collages of different lengths in a gallery
Two cells, a long collage (40 × 2 in, 24 panels) and a shorter one (24 × 2 in, 12 panels), joined by group. Each opens at screen height from its left end; stepping to the other image fits it afresh, so the short collage doesn’t keep the long one’s scale or position. Whether a figure counts as a strip depends only on its shape (much shorter, and the short one would open whole on the test’s 2560 px wide screen), so fig-dpi: 48 halves the resolution to keep the files small. The captions differ in length: stepping between the two changes the caption band’s height, and each collage must stay clear of it.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   group: mixed-collages
#| fig-width: 40
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-dpi: 48
#| fig-cap: "The long collage."

collage(n = 24)
```




The long collage.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   group: mixed-collages
#|   description: "A longer text under the short collage, so that the caption band grows when the gallery steps to it. Each panel is a random walk of 200 steps, coloured along a single palette from the first panel to the last, and titled with its panel number so the order can be read at any zoom."
#| fig-width: 24
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-dpi: 48
#| fig-cap: "The short collage, with a description."

collage(n = 12)
```




The short collage, with a description.





A longer text under the short collage, so that the caption band grows when the gallery steps to it. Each panel is a random walk of 200 steps, coloured along a single palette from the first panel to the last, and titled with its panel number so the order can be read at any zoom.

title: K: Python, panzoom: true with the lightbox
text:
NoteAbout this page



This page tests panzoom: true with the Jupyter engine, next to Quarto’s lightbox: true. The cases are the same as on J, the lightbox-only reference: panzoom should take every image the lightbox takes on J, except where a case asks for the lightbox explicitly. The knitr equivalent is page C.
Keep the cases in step with the other page of the pair. Each heading’s expect-open says what should open. Jupyter leaves the panzoom and lightbox options out of the code shown on the page; the Code button at the top shows the full source.
The cases below share this setup:
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
```

title: K: Python, panzoom: true with the lightbox
text:
1. Figure with a caption

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(x))
plt.show()
```




A sine wave.

title: K: Python, panzoom: true with the lightbox
text:
2. Plot without a caption

```{python}
plt.plot(x, np.cos(x))
plt.show()
```

title: K: Python, panzoom: true with the lightbox
text:
3. Subfigures (fig-subcap, layout-ncol)
```{python}
#| label: fig-pair
#| fig-cap: Two waves.
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - Sine
#|   - Cosine
#| layout-ncol: 2

plt.plot(x, np.sin(2 * x))
plt.show()
plt.plot(x, np.cos(2 * x))
plt.show()
```











(a) Sine











(b) Cosine







Figure 1: Two waves.

title: K: Python, panzoom: true with the lightbox
text:
4. Nested lightbox: options
A cell’s own lightbox: options ask for Quarto’s lightbox, so panzoom leaves the cell to it, as with knitr (page C, cases 6 and 7). With Jupyter, Quarto’s lightbox ignores the options themselves: the group and description don’t reach it.

```{python}
plt.plot(x, np.sin(3 * x))
plt.show()
plt.plot(x, np.cos(3 * x))
plt.show()
```

title: K: Python, panzoom: true with the lightbox
text:
5. lightbox: false
Opted out of the lightbox; panzoom leaves an explicit lightbox setting alone too.

```{python}
plt.plot(x, np.sin(4 * x))
plt.show()
```

title: K: Python, panzoom: true with the lightbox
text:
6. panzoom: true on a cell
Without the panzoom filter (K) the option means nothing, and the document’s lightbox: true takes the plot.

```{python}
plt.plot(x, np.cos(4 * x))
plt.show()
```
